title: Smart Glasses Explained: Ray-Ban Meta and Beyond
description: What smart glasses do in plain English: cameras, open-ear audio, AI assistants and in-lens displays, plus privacy etiquette and UK and EU availability.
h1: Smart glasses explained: Ray-Ban Meta and beyond
intro: Smart glasses have gone from sci-fi to the For You page. Here’s what they actually do, the difference between models, and the etiquette of wearing a camera on your face.

image.alt: A MacBook, headphones and assorted accessories on a desk

cardText: Cameras, open-ear audio, AI and in-lens displays: what smart glasses do and where to get them.

sections.html: Most popular smart glasses, such as Ray-Ban Meta, look like ordinary frames but add a small camera for hands-free photos and point-of-view video, open-ear speakers for music and calls, and a voice assistant (Meta AI) you can ask questions. They don’t have a screen.

Meta Ray-Ban Display adds a small screen inside one lens for messages, directions and captions, and is controlled with a wristband. Meta paused its planned international rollout in early 2026 because of demand in the US, so check Meta’s or Ray-Ban’s site in your country for current availability.

• A light on the frame shows when you’re recording, but people may not notice it. Ask before filming people close up.
  • Many venues, gyms, schools and workplaces don’t allow recording; take them off where cameras aren’t welcome.
  • Review the app’s privacy settings, including how AI features use your photos and voice.

Great for cyclists, runners, parents capturing moments hands-free, and creators filming point-of-view clips. If you mainly want audio, open-ear headphones are cheaper. Compare them in the phones and wearables finder.
